summary:
We developed Earth System Trend Detective, an interactive dashboard that turns NASA satellite observations into understandable evidence of environmental change. Our Phoenix, Arizona prototype analyzes monthly nighttime land surface temperatures from 2003–2024, letting users explore charts, compare four subregions, and investigate local warming patterns.

The project addresses the challenge by combining quality-checked NASA MODIS data with statistical methods that account for seasonal temperature cycles, revealing long-term trends that summer–winter fluctuations can obscure. Plain-language summaries and traceable evidence help users understand both the findings and their limitations. Across the four Phoenix subregions, estimated warming ranges from approximately 0.06°C to 0.11°C per year.

This matters because satellite datasets can be difficult to interpret without specialized expertise. By making Earth observations accessible and transparent, our tool helps students, researchers, and communities investigate environmental change, ask better questions, and build an evidence-based understanding of their surroundings.
details:
Earth System Trend Detective transforms NASA satellite observations into an interactive investigation of environmental change. Developed for the “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge, our prototype explores nighttime land surface temperatures across Phoenix, Arizona, from 2003 through 2024. It helps users move from viewing measurements to asking scientific questions, comparing locations, and understanding the evidence behind a warming trend.

The project uses NASA Terra/MODIS MOD11C3 Collection 6.1 monthly observations. Our data pipeline screens measurements using quality flags, converts accepted values into degrees Celsius, and calculates regional averages. The Phoenix study window is divided into four subregions, allowing users to compare patterns across the area. Measurements that fail coverage requirements remain missing rather than being replaced with invented values. Temperature anomalies show how each month differs from its corresponding calendar-month average across the study period.

To investigate long-term change, we apply the seasonal Mann-Kendall test and seasonal Sen’s slope. These methods account for recurring seasonal variation, helping reveal warming that large summer-to-winter temperature swings can obscure. All four subregions show statistically significant warming, with estimated rates ranging from approximately 0.06°C to 0.11°C per year. Interactive charts and automatic plain-language summaries make these results understandable without requiring users to interpret statistical outputs alone.

Our discovery prototype adds a question-driven investigation workflow. Users can identify the fastest-warming subregion, compare a satellite grid cell with its surrounding region, or explore whether warming has accelerated. The system retrieves local evidence, performs predefined calculations, and displays its sources and operations. When evidence cannot support a conclusion, it says so. For example, the acceleration investigation remains inconclusive because comparing two slopes alone does not establish a statistically significant change.

We developed the project primarily in Python, using pandas for data processing, pymannkendall for trend analysis, and Pydantic for structured validation. FastAPI serves the results, while Streamlit and Plotly power the interactive dashboard. Render hosts the dashboard and API. Pytest, Ruff, Docker, and GitHub Actions support testing, consistency, and deployment. An offline option makes the project usable when internet access is unavailable.

The project’s creativity lies in connecting satellite data, statistical investigation, and accessible storytelling within one experience. Rather than presenting a single warming statistic, it invites users to investigate differences across places and examine the evidence themselves. The current discovery workflow is deterministic; optional Gemini integration can generate explanations during processing, but the committed release uses automatic summaries grounded in computed results.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, reproducibility, data provenance, missing observations, and reliable demonstrations. We distinguish land surface temperature from air temperature and avoid presenting trends as causes or forecasts. We also disclose that exploratory local comparisons do not prove significant differences between locations.

The intended impact is to make Earth observation more approachable for students, educators, researchers, and communities. By showing both what the data reveals and what remains uncertain, Earth System Trend Detective encourages informed curiosity and responsible interpretation. Phoenix provides a focused demonstration of an approach that could eventually support broader geographic investigations and help more people engage directly with evidence of environmental change.
